messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Fisherman
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 65

# Marcus's Story

Marcus has spent forty-three years on the water. His weathered hands know the rhythm of nets and rope the way most men know their own breathing. At fifty-eight, he moves across his fishing boat with the unconscious grace of someone who has made peace with the ocean—or so he thought.

Three months ago, everything changed. Marcus was working alone on a calm morning in late August, his small commercial vessel anchored in familiar waters where he has fished since he was fifteen. He was hauling nets, a task he performs dozens of times each week without thinking. The weather was clear. The sea was cooperative. There was no warning.

A larger cargo vessel appeared on the horizon, moving faster than Marcus realized. He didn't hear it coming—his hearing isn't what it once was, and the sound of his own equipment masked the approaching engine. When he finally looked up, the massive ship was already too close. Marcus has replayed those seconds countless times since: the moment of recognition, the futile wave of his arms, the sickening realization that he couldn't move his boat fast enough.

The cargo vessel struck Marcus's boat broadside. The impact threw him across the deck, his body slamming against the metal rail. He remembers the sound of splintering wood, the sudden cold of the ocean, the desperate scramble to stay above water as his boat sank beneath him. A fishing vessel nearby pulled him from the water after what felt like hours but was probably closer to fifteen minutes. He had a fractured rib, a concussion, and severe lacerations on his left leg. The physical injuries have mostly healed.

The rest hasn't.

Marcus hasn't returned to fishing. He tells people it's because of the rib, because he's waiting for the insurance settlement, because the boat needs repairs. These things are true, but they're not the real reason. The real reason is that he can't go back.

He lies awake most nights, his mind replaying the collision. Around 3 a.m., he usually gives up on sleep and sits on his small patio, watching the dark water in the distance. When he does sleep, he dreams of drowning—not the way it actually happened, but in variations that feel disturbingly real. Sometimes the water is above his head before he realizes he's in it. Sometimes the rescue never comes.

During the day, Marcus moves through his house like a ghost. His daughter calls frequently, worried. He tells her he's fine, that he just needs time. But he startles at loud noises—the garbage truck, the neighbor's power tools, the sound of a large engine anywhere nearby. His chest tightens and his breathing becomes shallow. Last week, a news report about a maritime accident came on the television, and Marcus felt such an overwhelming surge of panic that he had to leave the room.

He's become hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. When he walks near the water, he scans the horizon obsessively, checking for approaching vessels. He avoids the harbor entirely now. He can't watch the news. Certain smells—salt water, diesel fuel, the particular mustiness of the marina—trigger a cascade of physical sensations: racing heart, trembling hands, a suffocating sense of dread.

Marcus knows intellectually that he was lucky. He survived. But survival, he's learning, is sometimes more complicated than the accident itself. The man who spent four decades finding peace in solitude on the ocean now feels profoundly unsafe in the very place that defined him. He sits in his living room, staring out the window toward the water he can no longer reach, wondering if the fisherman he was will ever recognize himself again.
